topics.title: Evolution of EBP & Its Links to Nursing Concepts
topics.summary: Evidence-based practice blends the best current research evidence, the nurse’s clinical expertise, and the client’s preferences; it grew from Nightingale’s data-driven reforms into a professional, legal, and quality expectation for every nurse.
objectives: Define evidence-based practice and name its three core components, explaining what each contributes to a clinical decision.
Distinguish research, evidence, and nursing experience, and explain why none of them alone is evidence-based practice.
Summarize the evolution of EBP from Florence Nightingale through Archie Cochrane, David Sackett, and the Institute of Medicine reports.
Explain translational research, the 17-year lag time, and the strategies that overcome “we’ve always done it that way.”
Relate EBP to accountability, clinical decision making, health promotion, legal standards, professionalism, and quality improvement.
Apply client preferences, culture, integrative health, and cost-conscious care when choosing an evidence-based intervention.
Use the COPD oxygen example to recognize when a tradition has been replaced by current evidence.
topics.bigPicture:
Every day at the bedside you will hear some version of “this is how we do it here.” Evidence-based practice (EBP) is the habit of asking why, checking whether that answer is supported by the best current evidence, and then fitting that evidence to this client, with your clinical judgment. It is not a research project you do once in school. It is the reason you no longer massage reddened bony prominences, the reason chlorhexidine bathing and central-line bundles exist, and the reason you do not withhold oxygen from a hypoxemic client with COPD out of fear of “knocking out the drive to breathe.”

EBP has three legs: best evidence, clinical expertise, and client preferences and values. Remove any leg and the stool tips. Evidence without judgment ignores how this client is actually doing. Judgment without evidence is tradition. Evidence and judgment without the client’s values ignore autonomy, which is a legal and ethical right.

On the NCLEX, EBP rarely appears as “define EBP.” It appears as a nurse who cites tradition, a new graduate who wants to change a policy alone, a client who declines a recommended treatment, or a standard of care that a nurse failed to meet. Your job is to recognize the response that integrates all three legs, respects the client, follows current standards, and uses the correct channel for change.

keyTerms.def: A problem-solving approach that blends research and evidence with nursing experience to make clinical decisions; in practice it integrates the best current evidence, the nurse’s clinical expertise, and the client’s preferences and values.
A formal, systematic way of answering a question or approaching a problem.
Acquired nursing knowledge based on formal, systematic studies or expert opinion.
The progressive and continuous development of knowledge, skills, and behaviors that builds proficiency in making clinical judgments about nursing care.

Clinical decision making that integrates three core components: (1) the best evidence from the most current research available, (2) the nurse’s clinical expertise, and (3) the client’s preferences, which reflect values, needs, interests, and choices.

The conscientious, explicit, and judicious use of current best external evidence together with individual clinical expertise to make decisions about the care of individual patients (Sackett and colleagues, 1990s).

A systematic approach to converting research knowledge into applications of health care that improve client outcomes (“bench to bedside”); new evidence currently takes an average of 17 years to reach routine clinical use.
The average time between identification of new evidence and its active use in clinical practice.

keyTerms.term: Clinical and Translational Science Awards (CTSA) Consortium
keyTerms.def: The NIH-supported network that funds and promotes translational (“bench to bedside”) research.
Landmark Institute of Medicine report on health care deficits that cause preventable harm; recommended EBP to reduce inappropriate variation and standardize safe, quality care.

keyTerms.term: The Future of Nursing: Leading Change, Advancing Health (IOM, 2011)

International organization inspired by Archie Cochrane that produces systematic reviews of health care interventions; Cochrane argued that care should be based on randomized controlled trials.
A person who leads or models a practice change, educates peers, and helps a unit replace outdated traditions with evidence-based care.

A continuous, data-driven process of improving the why, when, and what of care at a specific setting using current evidence to deliver safe, effective interventions.
The values, needs, interests, health beliefs, culture, spirituality, and choices that shape what care a client accepts, declines, or prioritizes.
The client’s right to self-determination, including the right to accept treatment, refuse treatment, seek a second opinion, and establish advance directives.
An approach that combines complementary health practices (such as mindfulness or acupuncture) with conventional medical care in a coordinated, interprofessional, holistic way.
Choosing effective interventions while considering availability, reimbursement requirements, and cost to the client and system.

The older belief that supplemental oxygen would suppress breathing and cause respiratory failure in clients with hypercapnic COPD; current evidence supports controlled, titrated oxygen with blood gas monitoring rather than withholding oxygen.

sections.heading: What EBP actually is: three legs, one decision
sections.body:
Evidence-based practice is a decision-making method, not a single fact. When a nurse uses EBP, three inputs are on the table at the same time. Best evidence answers “What has been shown to work, in whom, and how well?” Clinical expertise answers “What do my assessment findings and experience tell me about this client right now?” Client preferences answer “What does this person value, believe, and choose?”

Why all three? Research is done on groups. Your client is one person, with a specific body, a specific set of risks, and a specific culture and set of goals. Evidence tells you what usually works; your assessment tells you whether this client fits the evidence (for example, whether an exclusion criterion such as a bleeding disorder applies); the client tells you whether the plan is acceptable. A plan that ignores any of the three is not EBP, even if it cites a famous study.

Notice what EBP is not. It is not “whatever the most experienced nurse does,” not “what the last hospital I worked at did,” and not “the newest article I read on social media.” It is also not a recipe that overrides the client: if evidence strongly supports a treatment and an informed adult with capacity declines it, EBP still respects that decision and looks for the best acceptable alternative.
sections.analogy: Think of a three-legged stool. Evidence is one leg, your clinical judgment is the second, and the client’s values are the third. A two-legged stool can look sturdy for a moment, but the minute someone sits on it, it falls. Clinical decisions are the person sitting on the stool.

check.q: A nurse says, “The research shows early ambulation reduces complications, so I will get the client up now even though they just became dizzy and hypotensive.” Which EBP leg is being ignored?
check.a: Clinical expertise (assessment). The evidence is sound for the population, but the nurse’s current assessment shows the client is unsafe to ambulate right now. EBP means applying evidence through clinical judgment, so the nurse should assess and stabilize first, then mobilize when safe.

sections.heading: Research, evidence, and experience: related but not the same
sections.body:
The vocabulary in this module is precise, and NCLEX-style items sometimes hinge on it. Research is the process: a formal, systematic way to answer a question. Evidence is the product nurses can use: knowledge from systematic studies, and when studies are lacking, expert opinion. Nursing experience is the clinician’s growing knowledge, skill, and behavior that builds clinical judgment over time.

EBP is the blend. A nurse who conducts research is generating new knowledge. A nurse who practices EBP is using the best available knowledge, filtered through experience and matched to the client. Most bedside nurses will practice EBP every shift and may never run a formal research study, and that is exactly the expectation for a new RN.

rows: Research
A systematic process for answering a question
A team randomly assigns post-op clients to two pain-reassessment intervals and measures outcomes.
Evidence
Knowledge from studies or expert opinion
A published systematic review shows chlorhexidine bathing reduces central-line infections.
Nursing experience
Progressive knowledge, skill, and judgment
A nurse recognizes a subtle change in a client’s breathing pattern before the monitor alarms.
Evidence-based practice
Integration of evidence, expertise, and client preference
The nurse uses the review, assesses the client’s skin, and honors the client’s preference about bathing time.

check.q: A nurse says, “I have worked on this unit for 15 years, so my way of doing dressing changes is evidence-based.” Is she correct?
check.a: Not by itself. Fifteen years of experience is nursing experience (clinical expertise), one leg of EBP. It becomes EBP only when her technique is also supported by current evidence (studies, guidelines, or facility policy built on them) and fitted to each client’s preferences. Experience alone, unchecked against evidence, can simply be tradition.

sections.heading: How EBP evolved: from Nightingale to the IOM
sections.body:
Florence Nightingale (1850s), the first nurse theorist, is the profession’s first evidence-based practitioner. In the Crimean War hospitals she noticed that soldiers in filthy, poorly ventilated wards died at high rates. She collected and analyzed mortality data, formed a hypothesis that sanitation mattered, tested it by introducing lighting, ventilation, hygiene, better diet, and cleanliness, and showed that infections fell and survival rose. Then she presented her findings to others so practice would change. Every part of modern EBP is visible in that sequence.

Dr. Archie Cochrane, a British epidemiologist, criticized medicine in the early 1970s for using interventions that had never been tested. He argued that randomized controlled trials (RCTs) should guide care; his work inspired the international Cochrane Collaboration, which produces systematic reviews still used today. In the 1990s, Dr. David Sackett and clinical epidemiologists at McMaster University popularized and defined evidence-based medicine: the conscientious, explicit, and judicious use of current best evidence together with clinical expertise.

Two Institute of Medicine (IOM) reports pushed EBP into health policy. Crossing the Quality Chasm (2001) documented that care in the United States was causing preventable harm and varied widely; it recommended EBP to reduce inappropriate variation and standardize safe, quality care. The Future of Nursing (2011) called for academic and practice changes so nurses could improve safety, quality, and outcomes through care coordination, health promotion, quality improvement, and EBP.

rows: Florence Nightingale
1850s, Crimean War
Used observation and mortality data to prove sanitation saves lives
First nurse to use data to change care
Archie Cochrane
Early 1970s
Criticized untested care; championed RCTs; inspired the Cochrane Collaboration
“Cochrane = controlled trials”
David Sackett & colleagues
Defined evidence-based medicine: best evidence plus clinical expertise
“Sackett set the definition”
IOM, Crossing the Quality Chasm
Preventable harm; EBP to reduce variation and standardize safe care
Chasm = gap in quality
IOM, The Future of Nursing
Nursing education and practice changes; EBP, QI, coordination, health promotion

steps: Make observations (high death rates in dirty wards).
Collect data (mortality records).
Analyze the data (deaths cluster with poor sanitation).
Develop a hypothesis (sanitation improves survival).
Test the hypothesis with new data (introduce ventilation, hygiene, diet, cleanliness; recount deaths).
Form a conclusion (sanitation reduces infection and death).
Summarize and present the process to others so practice changes.

check.q: Which step of Nightingale’s process is most often skipped by modern units that try a new practice informally?
check.a: Testing with new data and presenting the results. Units frequently adopt a change and never measure outcomes or share them. Without outcome data, no one knows whether the change helped, harmed, or did nothing.

sections.heading: Translational research and the 17-year gap
sections.body:
Translational research is the systematic process of moving research findings into real clinical use, often summarized as “bench to bedside.” The National Institutes of Health (NIH) supports it through the Clinical and Translational Science Awards (CTSA) Consortium. The need is real: it currently takes an average of 17 years for new evidence to become routine practice. During that lag, clients receive care that is less effective than it could be.

Why so slow? Busy clinicians may not have time to read research, may not know how to appraise it, or may work in a culture where tradition is defended (“we’ve always done it that way”). Policies take time to revise, equipment must be purchased, and staff must be educated. Some resistance is healthy, because not every new study should change practice, but much of it is simply habit.

Closing the gap takes deliberate work: teamwork, change agents and patient-care champions who model the new practice, staff education, and client education so clients understand and expect the evidence-based approach. The guiding rule is that a change must improve care without weakening safety or quality; it should be piloted, monitored, and evaluated rather than imposed overnight.
bullets: Barrier: tradition and habit. Strategy: present the evidence and invite discussion; use champions who are respected peers.
Barrier: lack of time or skill to appraise research. Strategy: staff education, journal clubs, access to librarians and databases.
Barrier: lack of resources. Strategy: involve leadership early and show cost and outcome data.
Barrier: fear the change is unsafe. Strategy: pilot test on one unit, audit outcomes, and adjust.
sections.example: On a medical unit, nurses routinely check residual gastric volume every four hours and hold tube feedings for any residual over 150 mL “because we always have.” A nurse champion brings current guidelines showing that routine holding at low residual volumes increases underfeeding without reducing aspiration in most adults. Rather than telling peers they are wrong, she shares the evidence at a staff meeting, the unit council brings it to the policy committee, and the unit pilots a revised protocol while tracking feeding goals and aspiration events.

check.q: Staff on a unit resist a new evidence-based bathing protocol, saying, “We’ve always done it this way, and nobody has gotten hurt.” Which strategies does the nurse leader use first, and which approach should be avoided?
check.a: Use teamwork and respected peer champions, educate staff on the evidence and the reason for the change, teach clients what to expect, and pilot the change on one unit while monitoring outcomes and safety. Avoid mandating the change overnight or dismissing staff concerns; concerns can reveal real safety issues, and buy-in is what makes the change last.

sections.heading: EBP connects to the rest of professional nursing
sections.body: EBP is not a stand-alone topic. It is woven into nearly every professional concept you study. The table below links each concept to EBP and to what you would actually do. Pay special attention to legal issues: the standard of care that juries and boards use to judge a nurse is built from clinical knowledge, expert opinion, and research. When practice changes because evidence changes, the standard of care changes too, and continuing an outdated practice can become a deviation from the standard.

rows: Accountability
Best-practice standards, responsibility, and scope of practice reflect EBP
The nurse is responsible for giving the best, most current care, which means staying current.
Clinical decision making
EBP supplies the scientific support for clinical thinking and judgment
Nurses use current best practice in each phase of the plan of care.
Health, wellness, and illness
Routine habits (sleep, hygiene, exercise) affect present and future health
Teach evidence-based self-care that promotes health and lowers risk.
Legal issues
Clinical knowledge, expert opinion, and research form professional standards
Conduct that deviates from professional standards can constitute malpractice.
Professional behaviors
A credible discipline must use EBP
Integrate best evidence with clinical experience and client preferences.
Quality improvement
Continuous improvement using current evidence
Improving the why, when, and what of care changes how care is delivered.

check.q: A nurse continues to use a wound-care method the facility retired two years ago because newer evidence showed it delays healing. The client’s wound worsens. Which concept is most directly at issue?
check.a: Legal issues and accountability. The current standard of care reflects the newer evidence; deviating from it and causing harm meets the elements of negligence or malpractice. The nurse is accountable for knowing and following current standards and policy.

sections.heading: Client preferences, culture, integrative health, and cost
sections.body:
The third leg of EBP is the client. Health beliefs, culture, spirituality, and family traditions shape what clients accept. An adult with decision-making capacity has the right to agree to a treatment (for example, supplemental oxygen), to refuse treatment (for example, a blood transfusion for religious reasons), to seek a second opinion, and to establish advance directives. Respecting a refusal is not a failure of EBP; it is EBP. The nurse’s job is to make sure the decision is informed, to explore the reasons with therapeutic communication, to notify the provider, to document, and to offer evidence-based alternatives the client will accept (such as blood-conservation strategies).

Integrative health combines complementary approaches such as mindfulness, yoga, massage, or acupuncture with conventional care, coordinated across professions. Research cited in this module followed nearly 500 clients with breast or gynecologic cancer who used integrative therapies and found improvement in appetite, fatigue, anxiety, pain, sleep, and overall well-being. The nursing role is to ask about complementary practices, look at the evidence and safety (including interactions, such as herbs and anticoagulants), and help the client integrate them with the medical plan rather than dismissing them or letting them replace effective treatment.

Cost-conscious care means choosing interventions that work and are available, while considering reimbursement rules and what the client can afford. An evidence-based dressing that the client cannot obtain after discharge will not heal the wound. Advocacy here sounds like: “This option has strong evidence; let me check whether it is covered or whether case management can help, and if not, which equally effective option is available.”
sections.example: A client with heart failure is taught to weigh daily and limit sodium, both evidence-based. The client says, “I can’t afford a scale, and my family always cooks with salted pork for church dinners.” The nurse does not repeat the same teaching louder. She asks the social worker about a free scale, explores which dishes matter most, teaches label reading and lower-sodium substitutions that keep the meal culturally meaningful, and documents the plan. Evidence, judgment, and preference have all been integrated.

check.q: A client with cancer asks whether acupuncture could help her nausea in addition to her antiemetics. Which response best reflects integrative, evidence-based care?
check.a: Acknowledge the interest, explain that some evidence supports acupuncture or acupressure as an addition to (not a replacement for) antiemetics, and offer to discuss it with the provider and team so it can be coordinated safely. Dismissing it ignores preference; endorsing it as a replacement ignores evidence.

sections.heading: Box 45.1 in action: oxygen for clients with COPD
sections.body:
This example shows how EBP replaces a tradition. For decades, nurses were taught the hypoxic drive theory: clients with chronic hypercapnic COPD breathe because of low oxygen, so giving oxygen would “take away the drive” and cause respiratory arrest. Fear of that outcome led some nurses to withhold or severely restrict oxygen even when clients were dangerously hypoxemic.

Current evidence shows that hypoxemia itself is the immediate danger. The rise in carbon dioxide that can occur with uncontrolled, high-concentration oxygen is mostly explained by ventilation-perfusion changes and the Haldane effect, not by loss of a “drive.” The evidence-based approach is controlled, titrated oxygen: give supplemental oxygen to clients whose saturation is at or below 88%, titrate to a target range of about 88% to 92% (or the range the provider orders), and monitor arterial blood gases frequently to make sure oxygenation is adequate without worsening carbon dioxide retention or acidosis.

The NCLEX lesson: never withhold oxygen from a hypoxemic client because of COPD. Give oxygen, titrate to the ordered target, and monitor for rising PaCO2, falling pH, and decreasing level of consciousness.

rows: Avoid oxygen in COPD; it will stop the client’s breathing
Give oxygen when SpO2 is 88% or less; hypoxemia is the more immediate threat
Low flow is always safe; high flow is always dangerous
Titrate to a target saturation (about 88–92%) rather than to a fixed flow
Watch the saturation only
Monitor ABGs frequently for PaCO2 and pH, plus mental status and work of breathing

check.q: A client with chronic hypercapnic COPD has an SpO2 of 82% and is anxious and tachypneic. A colleague says, “Don’t put oxygen on, he’s a CO2 retainer.” What should the nurse do?
check.a: Apply oxygen as ordered (or per protocol), titrate to the target range of about 88–92%, and monitor ABGs, mental status, and respiratory effort. Withholding oxygen leaves the client hypoxemic, which is the immediate life threat.

sections.heading: Common traps & look-alikes
sections.body: These pairs are where students lose points. Read the clue column: it is the detail in a stem that tells you which concept is being tested.

rows: Research vs EBP
Research generates new knowledge with a formal study; EBP applies existing best evidence to care
“Collect data from participants to test a hypothesis” = research; “find and apply the best evidence” = EBP
Evidence vs experience
Evidence comes from systematic studies or expert opinion; experience is the individual nurse’s growing judgment
“Studies show…” vs “In my years on this unit…”
EBP vs tradition
EBP is supported by current evidence; tradition is supported by habit
“We’ve always done it this way” signals tradition, not evidence
EBP vs quality improvement
QI uses local data to improve processes in one setting; EBP brings external evidence into practice; they often work together
Audits, run charts, PDSA cycles = QI; literature search and appraisal = EBP
Respecting refusal vs abandoning EBP
Honoring an informed refusal is part of EBP; failing to inform the client or offer alternatives is not
Look for “explore the reason, inform, notify provider, offer alternatives”
Cochrane vs Sackett
Cochrane championed RCTs (1970s); Sackett defined evidence-based medicine (1990s)
“Randomized trials” vs “definition of EBM”
Crossing the Quality Chasm vs Future of Nursing
2001 report on preventable harm and variation; 2011 report on nursing education and practice
“Preventable harm, variation” vs “academic changes for nurses”

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: recognizing evidence-based reasoning
sections.body:
Items on this topic usually describe a nurse’s statement or action and ask you to judge it. Common patterns: “Which statement by the new nurse indicates a need for further teaching?” (the wrong one usually cites tradition, a single expert, or ignores the client); “Which action best demonstrates evidence-based practice?” (the right one integrates evidence, assessment, and preference); “A client declines a recommended treatment. What is the best response?” (the right one respects autonomy while informing and offering alternatives); and integrated items like the COPD oxygen scenario, where a physical safety need (hypoxemia) must win over an outdated belief.

Here is an original sample item. A senior nurse on a long-term care unit tells a new graduate, “We always massage reddened heels and hips because it brings blood flow back and residents like it.” The new graduate checks current pressure-injury prevention guidelines. Which action by the new graduate best reflects evidence-based practice? A. Continue massaging reddened areas because the senior nurse’s experience counts as evidence. B. Avoid massaging the reddened areas, offload and reposition per current guidelines, reassess the skin, and explain the change to the resident. C. Ask each resident whether they prefer massage and do whichever they choose. D. Stop all skin care until the unit completes its own research study on massage.
steps: Read the stem: a tradition (“we always massage…”) is in conflict with current guidelines, and the question asks for the action that best reflects EBP.
Identify what is being asked: the answer must integrate all three legs, evidence, clinical judgment, and client preference, not just one.

Spot cues: “always” and “residents like it” signal tradition and preference alone; “checks current guidelines” signals that the evidence leg is available. Current guidelines advise against massaging reddened bony prominences because it can damage already-stressed tissue.
Eliminate A: experience is one leg, but it does not override current evidence; following tradition is not EBP.
Eliminate C: preference matters, but offering a potentially harmful option as an equal choice without sharing evidence ignores the evidence leg and the duty to inform.
Eliminate D: EBP uses existing evidence; a unit does not need its own research study before applying well-established guidelines, and stopping skin care is unsafe.
Choose B: it applies current evidence, includes reassessment (clinical expertise), and involves the resident through explanation (preference and informed participation).

check.q: What reusable strategy does this item teach?
check.a: When an item asks for the “best” EBP action, look for the option that contains all three legs: evidence, assessment or judgment, and client involvement. Options built on only one leg (tradition, expert say-so, or preference alone) are distractors.

sections.heading: Worked case: a refusal, a tradition, and a new nurse
sections.body: Mr. Okafor, 68, is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia and has chronic hypercapnic COPD. His SpO2 is 85% on room air, respirations 28, and he is anxious. His orders include oxygen to keep SpO2 88–92% and an ABG in one hour. The night nurse at handoff says, “I kept him on room air. You know COPD clients, oxygen will knock out his drive.” Mr. Okafor also tells you he is a Jehovah’s Witness and will not accept blood products, even if he bleeds again (he had a GI bleed last year). He asks whether the breathing exercises the therapist mentioned are “real or just busywork.”
steps: Recognize cues: SpO2 85% with tachypnea and anxiety is hypoxemia, an immediate physiologic threat. The handoff statement reflects the outdated hypoxic drive theory.
Prioritize: airway and breathing come first. Apply oxygen now as ordered and titrate to 88–92%; do not wait to debate the colleague.
Monitor: reassess SpO2, respiratory rate and effort, and mental status; obtain the ordered ABG to check PaCO2 and pH. Report drowsiness, rising PaCO2, or worsening acidosis promptly.

Address the practice gap professionally: privately share the current evidence with the night nurse and, if this belief is common on the unit, bring it to the charge nurse or unit practice council for education. This is the champion role, not a confrontation.

Respect preference: Mr. Okafor’s refusal of blood is his right as an informed adult. Confirm he understands the risks, notify the provider, document, and ask whether he wants information on blood-conservation alternatives and his advance directive.
Teach with evidence: explain that breathing exercises and early mobility have evidence for improving secretion clearance and recovery, using plain language and teach-back.
Evaluate: one hour later, SpO2 is 90%, respirations 22, and the ABG shows a stable PaCO2. The plan integrated evidence, judgment, and preference.

check.q: In this case, which action came first, and why did it outrank correcting the colleague?
check.a: Applying and titrating oxygen came first because hypoxemia is an immediate breathing threat (ABCs). Peer education about the outdated belief is important but can safely wait until the client is stabilized.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
In North Carolina, nursing practice is regulated by the North Carolina Board of Nursing (NCBON) under the NC Nursing Practice Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 90, Article 9A, G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.). The RN’s components of practice are described in 21 NCAC 36 .0224, and the LPN’s in .0225. The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment, which means the RN is accountable for basing those functions on current, accepted standards. National bodies such as the ANA describe standards, but each state’s practice act defines the legal scope.

EBP and liability are connected in NC as everywhere: malpractice is judged against the standard of care, and the standard evolves with evidence. North Carolina’s medical malpractice statute of limitations is generally 3 years, with a 4-year statute of repose (G.S. 1-15(c)), and NC is one of the few jurisdictions that still recognizes pure contributory negligence as a defense. You will not be tested on those numbers on the NCLEX, but they explain why NC employers emphasize current policies, documentation, and staff education when practice changes.

North Carolina is a Nurse Licensure Compact state. If you practice on a multistate license in another compact state, you must follow that state’s practice act and the current standards where the client is located.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 45 study guide, Evidence-Based Practice, learning outcomes 45.1 and 45.2, key terms and Sections 2–3, pp. 2759–2761 (including Box 45.1 and the Focus on Integrative Health feature).

Clarification 1 (COPD oxygen, Box 45.1): The source states that oxygen is recommended for clients with SpO2 of 88% or less with frequent blood gases. Current guidance (GOLD and other respiratory guidelines) is to give controlled oxygen and titrate to a target SpO2 of about 88–92% in clients at risk for hypercapnia, using the provider’s ordered target; oxygen should never be withheld from a hypoxemic client. The guide teaches the target range.

Clarification 2 (history): Archie Cochrane’s influential book on effectiveness and efficiency was published in 1972 (the source lists 1971). The term “evidence-based medicine” is usually credited to Gordon Guyatt of the McMaster group (1991), with David Sackett and colleagues providing the widely cited 1996 definition; the source’s summary that Sackett and clinical epidemiologists coined and defined EBM in the 1990s is accepted in this guide.

Clarification 3 (organization names): The Institute of Medicine is now called the National Academy of Medicine (since 2015), and a follow-up report, The Future of Nursing 2020–2030, was published in 2021 with a focus on health equity. The 2001 and 2011 report findings in the source remain accurate.

mnemonics.name: E-C-P stool
mnemonics.text: Evidence + Clinical expertise + Preference = EBP. Missing a leg? It’s not EBP.

mnemonics.name: N-C-S-I-I timeline
mnemonics.text: Nightingale (1850s data) → Cochrane (1970s RCTs) → Sackett (1990s EBM) → IOM Chasm (2001) → IOM Future of Nursing (2011). “Nurses Can Study In Institutes.”

pearls: “We’ve always done it that way” is the classic NCLEX signal of tradition, not evidence; the correct answer usually involves checking current evidence or policy.
Expert opinion counts as evidence, but it ranks near the bottom of the hierarchy (only an individual’s personal opinion ranks lower); it does not override strong research.
Respecting an informed refusal is part of EBP. Inform, explore reasons, notify the provider, document, and offer alternatives.
Hypoxemia kills faster than hypercapnia: give oxygen to a hypoxemic client with COPD and titrate to about 88–92%.
The standard of care moves with the evidence; continuing a retired practice can be a deviation from the standard.
Change on a unit goes through champions, education, pilot testing, and committees, not through one nurse acting alone.
Integrative therapies are added to conventional care, coordinated by the team, and checked for safety and interactions.
redFlags: A colleague withholding oxygen from a hypoxemic client with COPD because of the hypoxic drive belief: intervene for the client first, then educate.
Overriding an informed, capable adult’s refusal because “the evidence says so” violates autonomy and can constitute battery.
Changing a unit-wide practice on your own based on one article bypasses policy, approval, and safety evaluation.
A client replacing effective treatment (such as chemotherapy or insulin) with an unproven complementary product needs prompt, nonjudgmental teaching and provider notification.
recap: EBP integrates best current evidence, clinical expertise, and client preferences; all three are required.
Research is the process, evidence is the product, experience is the clinician’s judgment, and EBP is the blend.
Nightingale used data to show sanitation saves lives; Cochrane championed RCTs; Sackett defined EBM; the IOM reports made EBP a quality expectation.
Translational research moves evidence from bench to bedside, but the average lag is about 17 years.
Teamwork, champions, staff education, and client education overcome tradition without weakening safety.
EBP underpins accountability, decision making, health promotion, legal standards, professionalism, and quality improvement.
Client autonomy, culture, integrative health choices, and cost shape how evidence is applied.
In COPD, give controlled oxygen to hypoxemic clients, titrate to the target range, and monitor ABGs.

checks.q: A nurse wants to stop using a practice the unit has done for 20 years after reading a strong systematic review. What is the best first step?
checks.a: Share the evidence with the nurse manager, educator, or unit practice council so it can be reviewed and taken through the policy process. Acting alone bypasses approval and safety evaluation; doing nothing ignores accountability.

checks.q: A client declines a recommended evidence-based treatment after a full explanation. Has the nurse failed to practice EBP?
checks.a: No. Client preference is one of the three components. The nurse confirms understanding, explores reasons, notifies the provider, documents, and offers acceptable alternatives.

checks.q: Two nurses argue: one cites a well-known physician’s opinion, the other cites a large RCT with conflicting results. Which carries more weight, and why?
checks.a: The large RCT. Expert opinion ranks near the bottom of the evidence hierarchy (just above an individual’s personal opinion), while a well-designed RCT is far stronger. Both nurses would still apply the evidence through clinical judgment and client preference.

checks.q: Why does the 17-year lag matter to a client?
checks.a: During the lag, clients receive care that is less effective or less safe than the evidence supports. Translational strategies shorten the time clients wait for better care.

checks.q: A client with COPD has an SpO2 of 86%. The provider ordered a target of 88–92%. What is the nursing action?
checks.a: Apply or increase oxygen per order to reach 88–92%, then monitor SpO2, ABGs, mental status, and work of breathing; avoid both withholding oxygen and over-oxygenating.

checks.q: A nurse is sued for using an outdated restraint practice. Which EBP-related concept will the court use to judge the nurse?
checks.a: The standard of care, built from current knowledge, expert opinion, and research. Deviating from it and causing harm can constitute malpractice.

topics.title: Research Methodology, Participants & Research Ethics
topics.summary: Nursing research uses the scientific method, quantitative or qualitative designs, and carefully selected, fully informed participants, all protected by IRBs, the Belmont Report principles, and HIPAA.
objectives: Distinguish nursing research from nursing clinical research and identify the scientific method steps in a scenario.
Choose quantitative or qualitative design based on the kind of question being asked and the data being collected.
Explain how inclusion and exclusion criteria protect both the validity of a study and the safety of participants.
Describe the nurse’s role in research informed consent, voluntary participation, and the right to withdraw.
Identify vulnerable populations and the role of the institutional review board (IRB).
Apply the Belmont Report principles of respect for persons, beneficence, and justice, plus HIPAA privacy protections, to clinical situations.
Describe the criteria that make nursing a profession and the sources of standards of nursing care.
topics.bigPicture:
Most of you will not run a large research study as new graduates, but many of you will care for clients who are enrolled in one. You may be the person a client turns to and says, “I signed something for a study and I don’t want to do it anymore,” or “The research nurse said I have to stay in.” Knowing research methods and research ethics is what lets you protect that client.

Research methods also explain the evidence you use. If you know the difference between a study that measures numbers (quantitative) and one that explores lived experience (qualitative), you know what kind of answer each can give. If you know why inclusion and exclusion criteria exist, you can recognize when a study’s results do or do not apply to the client in front of you.

On the NCLEX, this content shows up as ethics and advocacy questions: a participant who wants to withdraw, a client who was pressured to enroll, a vulnerable person whose consent is questionable, a breach of confidentiality, or a nurse unsure whether to answer a participant’s questions about the study. The correct answer protects the client’s rights first.

keyTerms.def: The use of a systematic and strict scientific process to analyze phenomena of interest to all areas of nursing, including practice, education, and administration.
Research that seeks answers to questions that will ultimately improve client care, such as comparing infection rates, wound care methods, or treatment efficacy.
A systematic process in which a question is asked about a phenomenon, data are collected, a hypothesis is formed, a study is planned and carried out, and a conclusion is presented (Box 45.2).
A testable prediction about the relationship between variables, formed from collected observations and tested in a study.
A characteristic or factor that can change or be measured in a study, such as bathing method (independent variable) and skin breakdown rate (dependent variable).
Research that uses precise measurement to collect numerical data and analyzes it statistically to describe findings or test relationships among variables.
Research that investigates a question through narrative data exploring the subjective experiences of people, with the goal of identifying patterns and themes.
Volunteers for a specific study who meet all the inclusion criteria, have been informed of all aspects of the study, and have given informed consent.
Characteristics (such as age, diagnosis, disease stage) a person must have to be eligible for a study so the sample represents the target population.
Characteristics (such as certain medications, conditions, or history) that disqualify a person from a study, often to protect safety or prevent confounding results.

A legal and ethical requirement giving volunteers the right to full disclosure of the study’s purpose, procedures, length, expectations, benefits, and risks before agreeing; usually written, obtained before the study begins, and revocable at any time.
A participant’s right to leave a study at any time without penalty or loss of the care to which they are otherwise entitled.
Pressure, threats, or excessive incentives that undermine voluntary participation; prohibited in ethical research.

Groups needing additional legal and ethical protection in research: human fetuses, neonates, children, prisoners, pregnant women (in federal rules), educationally disadvantaged people, and cognitively impaired people.
A child’s or cognitively impaired person’s affirmative agreement to participate, sought in addition to permission from a parent or legally authorized representative.
A committee that reviews research protocols before and during a study to ensure participants’ rights and welfare are protected and ethical standards are met.
The U.S. report that established three core ethical principles for human research: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.

Acknowledging and protecting individual autonomy, protecting those with diminished autonomy, ensuring voluntary participation without coercion, and providing full disclosure and the right to withdraw.
Protecting participants from physical injury, psychological harm, economic loss, and exploitation, maximizing benefit and minimizing risk, and conducting research for the benefit of others.
Fair treatment of participants, including fair selection and distribution of research burdens and benefits, and (as taught in nursing research) strict confidentiality and protection of anonymity.
Participant identity and data are known to the researchers but are protected and not disclosed.
Even the researchers cannot link data to a specific participant.
Federal rule setting national standards that protect the disclosure of individually identifiable health information, including during research.

Grants from professional and government organizations such as Sigma Theta Tau International, AHRQ, the National Institute of Nursing Research (NINR), NCSBN, the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, and the American Cancer Society.

keyTerms.term: Criteria for nursing as a profession
keyTerms.def: Specialized education, a well-defined body of knowledge and expertise, ongoing research, service orientation, a code of ethics, professional autonomy, and professional organization membership.

Expectations for competent practice defined nationally by organizations such as the ANA, NLN, and The Joint Commission, and legally defined by each state’s Nurse Practice Act through its Board of Nursing.

sections.heading: Why nursing does research, and who pays for it
sections.body:
Nursing research applies a strict, systematic scientific process to questions that matter to nursing in every setting: practice, education, and administration. A study on how to teach medication safety to students is nursing research; so is a study on nurse staffing and retention. Nursing clinical research is the subset focused on client care: comparing infection rates with two catheter-care protocols, testing wound dressings, or measuring whether a fall-prevention bundle works.

Research is also one of the criteria that make nursing a profession. A profession has specialized education, a well-defined body of knowledge, ongoing research that grows that knowledge, a service orientation, a code of ethics, autonomy, and professional organizations. Without research, nursing would rely only on borrowed knowledge and tradition.

Research costs money. Nurse researchers apply for grants from professional and government organizations: Sigma Theta Tau International (the nursing honor society), the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), the National Institute of Nursing Research (NINR), the National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN), the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, and the American Cancer Society. Knowing who funded a study also helps you evaluate it, because funding sources should be disclosed and conflicts of interest considered.

check.q: A nurse researcher studies how different orientation models affect new-graduate turnover. Is this nursing clinical research?
check.a: It is nursing research (administration and education), but not nursing clinical research, because the question focuses on staff outcomes rather than directly on client care outcomes.

sections.heading: The scientific method: the backbone of every study
sections.body:
Box 45.2 lists the general elements of the scientific method. Notice how closely they mirror Nightingale’s process from the first topic. Each step has a job. The question defines what you want to know. Data collection grounds the question in observation. The hypothesis is a testable prediction. The study or experiment tests that prediction under planned conditions. The conclusion reports whether the evidence supported the hypothesis and shares it so others can use or repeat it.

The order matters. A hypothesis that comes before any observation is a guess. A conclusion drawn without a planned study is an opinion. When NCLEX-style items describe a nurse researcher’s activity and ask which step it represents, match the action to the step’s job.
steps: Ask a question about a phenomenon (Why do more clients on our unit develop heel pressure injuries than on the unit next door?).
Collect information and data (Review skin assessments, bed types, turning schedules, and nutrition data).
Form a hypothesis from the findings (Clients who receive heel offloading boots will have fewer heel injuries than those who do not).
Plan and carry out the study (Assign clients to boots or standard care, measure injuries for 4 weeks).
Present a conclusion about the phenomenon (Report whether the boots reduced injuries and share the results).

check.q: A researcher writes, “Clients who use a bedside commode at night will have fewer falls than those who walk to the bathroom.” Which element of the scientific method is this?
check.a: A hypothesis: a testable prediction about the relationship between two variables (toileting method and falls).

sections.heading: Quantitative versus qualitative: numbers or narratives
sections.body:
The type of question decides the design. Quantitative research asks “how much,” “how many,” “how often,” or “does X cause or relate to Y?” It uses precise measurement (pain scores, infection rates, blood glucose values) and statistical analysis to describe findings or test relationships among variables. The source’s example compares skin breakdown rates in infants bathed with water alone versus soap: a measurable outcome in two groups.

Qualitative research asks “what is it like?” or “how do people experience this?” It collects narrative data through interviews, focus groups, observation, or journals, and analyzes it for patterns and themes. The source’s example explores coping and adjustment after radical mastectomy. Qualitative findings help nurses understand the client’s perspective, which directly supports the client-preference leg of EBP.

Neither is “better.” They answer different questions. In the evidence hierarchy, qualitative studies sit among non-experimental designs and are weaker for proving that an intervention works, but they are the right tool for understanding meaning, barriers, and experience.

sections.example: A nurse wants to know why clients on the cardiac unit stop taking their beta-blockers after discharge. She interviews 15 clients and finds repeated themes of fatigue, cost, and confusion about refills. That is qualitative research. If she next compares readmission rates between clients who receive a pharmacist call and clients who do not, that is quantitative.

check.q: A study asks parents to describe what helped them cope during their infant’s NICU stay. Which design is this, and what will the results look like?
check.a: Qualitative. Results will be themes (for example, “being included in care,” “consistent nurses”) drawn from narrative data, not statistics.

sections.heading: Choosing participants: inclusion, exclusion, and vulnerable groups
sections.body:
Research participants are volunteers who meet all the inclusion criteria, have been told about every aspect of the study, and have given informed consent. All three conditions must be met. A person who is eligible but not informed is not a valid participant; neither is a person who consented but does not meet criteria.

Inclusion criteria define who belongs in the study so the sample represents the target population (for example, adults 18–65 with type 2 diabetes for at least one year). Exclusion criteria remove people for whom the study could be unsafe or whose characteristics would confuse the results (for example, pregnancy, kidney failure, or taking a medication that interacts with the study drug). Typical qualifiers include age, gender, medical history, disease stage, and current medications. Criteria serve two purposes at once: they protect participants’ physical and psychosocial safety and they protect the study’s validity.

For the bedside nurse, criteria matter in two ways. First, if you learn that a participant has developed an exclusion condition (a new pregnancy, a new medication), report it to the research team and the provider. Second, when you read evidence, check whether your client resembles the study population; a trial that excluded adults over 75 may not apply cleanly to your 88-year-old client.

Vulnerable populations receive extra legal and ethical protection because their ability to give free, informed consent may be limited or because they could be exploited: human fetuses, neonates, children, prisoners, educationally disadvantaged individuals, and cognitively impaired individuals. Federal rules also give special protections to pregnant women. Research with these groups requires additional IRB review and, for children and adults lacking capacity, permission from a parent or legally authorized representative plus the person’s own assent whenever they are able to give it.

check.q: A prisoner is told he may get an earlier parole hearing if he joins a drug trial. Why is this a problem?
check.a: Prisoners are a vulnerable population because their liberty is restricted, which makes them easy to coerce. Linking parole to participation is coercion and violates respect for persons; the IRB would not approve it.

sections.heading: Informed consent in research and the IRB
sections.body:
Informed consent in research is both legal and ethical. Volunteers have the right to full disclosure of the study’s purpose, required procedures, length, expectations, and possible benefits and risks, before they agree. Consent is usually written and is obtained before the study begins. It is also ongoing: participants keep the right to ask questions and to withdraw at any time, without penalty and without losing the standard care they would otherwise receive.

Who does what? The principal investigator or designated research team member is responsible for explaining the study and obtaining consent, just as the provider is responsible for explaining a procedure. The bedside nurse’s role is advocacy: verify that the client understands, that participation is voluntary, and that questions are answered. If the client seems confused about the study, cannot state its basic purpose, or feels pressured, the nurse does not proceed with study procedures and notifies the investigator. If a client asks to withdraw, the nurse respects the request, reports it to the research team promptly, and reassures the client that regular care continues.

The institutional review board (IRB) protects participants at the system level. It reviews protocols before a study starts (risks, benefits, consent forms, recruitment methods, protections for vulnerable groups) and monitors studies during their conduct, including adverse events and protocol changes. No study involving human participants should begin without IRB approval. If a nurse has concerns about how a study is being conducted, the IRB is an appropriate place to report them after following the chain of command.

steps: Ask the client to tell you in their own words what the study involves and why they joined.
Listen for signs of misunderstanding (“They said I’d be cured”), pressure (“My doctor said I had to”), or wanting out (“I don’t want to do this anymore”).
If understanding is incomplete, hold study-specific procedures and notify the investigator to re-explain.
If the client wants to withdraw, honor it, notify the research team and provider, and reassure the client that regular care continues.
Document the client’s statements and the notifications made.

check.q: The nurse is asked to witness a client’s signature on a research consent form. The client says, “I don’t really know what this study is, but my doctor wants me in it.” What does the nurse do?
check.a: Hold the signing and ask the investigator to return and re-explain the study. The client lacks understanding and may feel pressured, so consent would not be informed or voluntary. The nurse does not explain the protocol in detail herself or ask family to decide; she verifies, advocates, notifies the investigator, and documents.

sections.heading: The Belmont Report, HIPAA, and privacy: protecting participants
sections.body:
Published in 1979 after research abuses such as the U.S. Public Health Service syphilis study at Tuskegee, the Belmont Report gives three principles that still underpin research regulations. The NCLEX will not ask you to recite the report, but it will describe a situation and expect you to recognize which right is at stake.

Respect for persons protects autonomy: participation must be voluntary, without coercion, with full disclosure and the right to withdraw. People with diminished autonomy (from disability, illness, restricted liberty, or immaturity) get extra protection. Beneficence means “do good and avoid harm”: protect participants from physical injury, psychological harm, economic loss, and exploitation; maximize benefit and minimize risk; and conduct research for the benefit of others. Justice means fairness: participants are selected fairly (not chosen because they are easy to access or less powerful), burdens and benefits are shared fairly, and, as nursing research texts teach, personal information is kept strictly confidential and anonymity is protected when promised.

The HIPAA Privacy Rule sets national standards for protecting individually identifiable health information, including when that information is used for research. In general, researchers need the participant’s authorization (or an IRB- or privacy-board-approved waiver, or properly de-identified data) to use protected health information. The minimum necessary information should be used, and it should be stored securely.

Two words are often confused. Confidentiality means the researchers know who the participant is but protect that information. Anonymity means no one, not even the researchers, can link the data to a person (for example, an unsigned paper survey with no codes). A study cannot promise anonymity if it collects names or medical record numbers; it can promise confidentiality.

rows: Respect for persons
Is participation informed and voluntary?
Telling a client their care will suffer if they leave a study
Plain-language consent; right to withdraw anytime
Beneficence
Are risks minimized and benefits maximized?
Continuing a study drug after a serious adverse effect appears
Data safety monitoring; stopping rules
Justice
Are participants chosen and treated fairly?
Recruiting only uninsured clients for a risky trial because they are easy to enroll

sections.analogy: Think of a study as a trip. Respect for persons is the ticket: the passenger chooses to go and may get off at any stop. Beneficence is the seat belt: the driver keeps the trip as safe as possible. Justice is the boarding line: everyone is treated fairly, and no one is pushed onto the bus because they had nowhere else to go.

check.q: A research assistant leaves a printed list of participants’ names and HIV status at the nurses’ station. Which protections are violated?
check.a: Confidentiality, protected under the justice principle as taught in nursing research and under the HIPAA Privacy Rule. The nurse should secure the document immediately and report the breach per policy.

bullets: Do not discuss a participant’s study data in public areas or with people outside the care or research team.
Do not access a participant’s chart out of curiosity, even if you are interested in the study.
Use coded identifiers on research forms when the protocol calls for it, and store forms in locked or secure electronic locations.
Report suspected breaches promptly through the facility’s privacy process.

sections.heading: Standards of nursing care and professional accountability
sections.body:
Research and evidence feed standards of nursing care. Nationally, standards are described by organizations such as the American Nurses Association (ANA), the National League for Nursing (NLN), and The Joint Commission (which sets accreditation standards for health care organizations). Legally, nursing standards and scope are defined by each state’s Nurse Practice Act and enforced by the state Board of Nursing.

Why does this belong in a research topic? Because the profession’s legitimacy depends on it. Nursing meets the criteria of a profession partly because it conducts ongoing research and follows a code of ethics. The ANA Code of Ethics also obligates nurses to protect the rights of research participants, which is why advocacy in research situations is a nursing responsibility, not a favor.

Think of standards as coming from three layers, each with a different job. Law is the outer boundary: the state Nurse Practice Act and the Board of Nursing rules say what an RN or LPN may legally do. Professional standards describe what competent practice looks like: ANA scope and standards, specialty organization guidelines (for example, the Oncology Nursing Society or the Wound, Ostomy and Continence Nurses Society), and accreditation standards from The Joint Commission that facilities must meet. Facility policies and procedures translate the evidence and the standards into the exact steps expected on your unit. When all three line up, the nurse simply follows policy. When they do not, the nurse never goes outside the law, and brings evidence-versus-policy gaps through the chain of command.

How is the standard of care used if something goes wrong? In a malpractice case or a Board complaint, the question is what a reasonably prudent nurse with similar education and experience would have done in the same situation. Evidence of that standard comes from the practice act, professional standards and guidelines, the facility’s own policies, textbooks and current research, and expert nurse testimony. That is why current evidence matters legally: as research changes the guidelines and the policy, it changes what “reasonably prudent” means.

check.q: A nurse asks, “If the ANA standard and my state’s Nurse Practice Act differ, which one legally defines my scope?” What is the answer?
check.a: The state Nurse Practice Act, as interpreted by the state Board of Nursing, legally defines scope of practice. Professional organization standards guide practice but do not have the force of law on their own.

steps: Ask: Is this activity within the legal scope of my license under my state’s Nurse Practice Act and Board rules? If not, stop.
Ask: Do I have the education and documented competence to do it safely?
Ask: Does facility policy allow it, and am I following the current version of that policy?
Ask: Is my action consistent with current evidence and professional standards for this client?
If any answer is “no” or “I am not sure,” do not proceed; consult the charge nurse, nurse manager, policy, or the Board’s scope-of-practice resources.
