sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: participant rights and advocacy
sections.body:
Expect scenario items where a research participant’s rights are threatened and you must pick the nurse’s best action or response. The right answer almost always protects autonomy (the right to information and to withdraw), protects from harm, or protects privacy, and it routes concerns to the investigator, the provider, and, when needed, the IRB. Distractors typically include persuading the client to stay, explaining the study yourself in detail, ignoring the concern because the consent is already signed, or breaching privacy to “help.”

Sample item: A client enrolled in a clinical trial for a new antihypertensive tells the nurse, “I signed the papers, but I’m scared of the side effects and want out. Will I still get treated for my blood pressure?” Which response by the nurse is best? A. “Because you signed the consent, you need to finish the study first.” B. “You can withdraw at any time, and your regular care will continue. I will let the research team and your provider know right away.” C. “The side effects are usually mild, so let’s give it another week.” D. “I’ll explain the study again so you can feel better about staying.”
steps: Read the stem: a participant has expressed a clear wish to withdraw and a fear about losing care.
Identify what is being asked: the best response, which means it must be both therapeutic and ethically correct.
Spot cues: “want out” is a withdrawal request; “will I still get treated” is a fear about penalty.
Eliminate A: signing consent does not remove the right to withdraw; this is false and coercive.
Eliminate C: minimizing side effects and asking for another week pressures the client and dismisses the concern.
Eliminate D: re-explaining to keep the client in the study is persuasion, and detailed study explanation is the investigator’s role.
Choose B: it states the right to withdraw, reassures that usual care continues (no penalty), and routes the request to the research team and provider.

check.q: What reusable strategy fits most research-ethics items?
check.a: Ask, “Whose right is at stake, and which option protects it right now?” Then prefer the option that honors the right and notifies the responsible person (investigator, provider, IRB) over options that persuade, delay, or ignore.

sections.heading: Worked case: a pediatric oncology study on the night shift
sections.body: You are caring for Maya, 9, who is enrolled with her mother’s written permission in a study comparing two mouth-care regimens to prevent chemotherapy-related mucositis. The protocol requires a mouth swab every 8 hours and a 0–10 pain rating. At 0200, Maya cries and says, “I don’t want the swab anymore. It hurts.” Her mother is asleep at the bedside. You also notice that the research assistant left the day’s data sheets, with participants’ names and room numbers, on the counter at the nurses’ station. A new nurse beside you says, “Just do the swab quickly; her mom already signed for it.”
steps: Recognize cues: Maya is a child (vulnerable population). Her mother gave permission, but Maya’s own assent matters and she is now dissenting. She is also reporting pain.
Analyze: in pediatric research, a child’s ongoing dissent to a research-only procedure should be respected; the new nurse’s reasoning ignores respect for persons.
Prioritize the client: assess Maya’s mouth and pain first. Oral pain from mucositis is a clinical problem that needs treatment regardless of the study.
Take action: hold the research swab, provide comfort and ordered analgesia, and when appropriate, talk with Maya’s mother about Maya’s wishes.
Communicate: notify the research team (per protocol, often the on-call investigator) and the provider of the dissent and the pain findings; document Maya’s statements.
Protect privacy: secure the data sheets immediately and report the confidentiality breach through the facility’s privacy process.

Teach: explain to the new nurse that signed permission does not remove a child’s right to have dissent heard or a participant’s right to withdraw, and that research procedures never take priority over the child’s comfort and safety.
Evaluate: Maya’s pain decreases to 3/10, the research team plans to discuss continuation with Maya and her mother in the morning, and the forms are secured.

check.q: Which two Belmont principles were most directly at risk in this case?
check.a: Respect for persons (Maya’s dissent and the right to withdraw) and justice/confidentiality (the exposed data sheets). Beneficence also applies because her pain had to be addressed before any study procedure.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
In North Carolina, the legal scope of nursing practice is set by the NC Nursing Practice Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 90, Article 9A, G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.) and enforced by the North Carolina Board of Nursing (NCBON). The RN components of practice (21 NCAC 36 .0224) make the RN accountable for assessment, planning, and evaluation, which includes recognizing when a research protocol activity conflicts with a client’s condition and reporting it. Professional organization standards (ANA, NLN, The Joint Commission) guide practice, but the Nurse Practice Act defines legal scope.

A caution about minors: G.S. 90-21.5 allows minors to consent to certain treatment services (sexually transmitted and other reportable diseases; pregnancy, except sterilization and abortion; substance or alcohol use; and emotional disturbance). That statute addresses health services, not research enrollment. Research involving minors follows federal human-subjects rules and IRB requirements, which generally require parental permission plus the child’s assent; follow the IRB-approved protocol and facility policy.

Confidentiality breaches are also a conduct issue. NCBON’s Just Culture–based approach separates human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior for practice events, but conduct issues such as confidentiality breaches are reportable to the Board rather than handled only by the employer.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 45 study guide, Evidence-Based Practice, learning outcome 45.3, key terms and Section 4, pp. 2762–2763 (including Box 45.2, the Belmont Report principles, vulnerable populations, IRBs, HIPAA, criteria for a profession, and standards of nursing care).

Clarification 1 (Belmont justice): The source lists confidentiality and anonymity under justice. In the original Belmont Report, justice centers on fair selection of participants and fair distribution of research burdens and benefits; privacy and confidentiality are protected through respect for persons and federal regulations. Nursing research texts commonly teach confidentiality under justice (“right to fair treatment and privacy”), so this guide presents both, and practice questions test fair selection as the defining feature of justice.

Clarification 2 (vulnerable populations): Federal human-subjects regulations also give special protections to pregnant women; this was added. Research with children requires parental permission plus the child’s assent when the child is capable.

Clarification 3 (consent roles): The source does not name who obtains research consent. This guide teaches the standard rule that the principal investigator or trained research staff obtains consent and the bedside nurse verifies understanding and advocates.

mnemonics.name: R-B-J: “Rights Before Journals”
mnemonics.text: Respect for persons (choice and withdrawal), Beneficence (do good, avoid harm), Justice (fair selection and fair treatment). Participants’ rights come before getting the data published.

mnemonics.name: Q-Q: “Quantity vs Quality of experience”
mnemonics.text: Quantitative counts quantities (numbers, statistics). Qualitative explores the quality of experience (words, themes).

pearls: A participant may withdraw at any time, even after signing consent, with no loss of usual care.
The investigator obtains research consent; the nurse verifies understanding, voluntariness, and advocates.
Clinical safety outranks the protocol: assess and treat the client before performing any research-only procedure.
Prisoners, children, neonates, fetuses, cognitively impaired, and educationally disadvantaged people need extra protection; pregnant women are also protected under federal rules.
Coercion includes subtle pressure, such as linking participation to better care, privileges, or excessive payment.
Confidential means “we know who you are but won’t tell”; anonymous means “no one can tell who you are.”
Qualitative research is the right design for understanding experience and meaning; quantitative for measuring effect.
redFlags: A participant states they want to withdraw and staff tell them they cannot: intervene, honor the request, and notify the investigator.
A client who cannot explain the study or appears confused about consent: hold study procedures and notify the investigator.
A participant develops a serious adverse effect: assess, provide care, and report to the provider and research team immediately.
Identifiable research data left in public view or shared without authorization: secure it and report the breach.
Recruitment that targets a group because they are easy to pressure (prisoners, uninsured, cognitively impaired) violates justice.
recap: Nursing research covers practice, education, and administration; nursing clinical research focuses on client care outcomes.
The scientific method moves from question to data to hypothesis to study to conclusion.
Quantitative research measures and analyzes numbers; qualitative research explores experience through narrative themes.
Participants must meet inclusion criteria, be fully informed, and give informed consent; exclusion criteria protect safety and validity.
Research consent is obtained by the investigator, is usually written, occurs before the study, and can be withdrawn at any time.
IRBs review and monitor studies; vulnerable populations receive added protection.
Belmont: respect for persons, beneficence, justice; HIPAA protects health information in research.
Standards of care come from national organizations and, legally, from each state’s Nurse Practice Act.

checks.q: A nurse researcher plans a study and wants to exclude clients taking anticoagulants. What is the most likely reason?
checks.a: Participant safety (and preventing confounding results). Exclusion criteria remove people for whom the intervention may be risky or whose condition could distort outcomes.

checks.q: A participant asks you detailed questions about how randomization works in her study. What should you do?
checks.a: Answer basic questions within your knowledge, then notify the investigator or research nurse to provide full information; verifying understanding is your role, while explaining the protocol in depth is the research team’s.

checks.q: A survey on nurse burnout is mailed with no names or codes. Can the researchers promise confidentiality or anonymity?
checks.a: Anonymity, because no one, including the researchers, can link responses to individuals.

checks.q: An adult with moderate dementia is enrolled after his daughter signs. During a study visit he repeatedly says “no” and pulls away. What principle guides the nurse?
checks.a: Respect for persons. People with diminished autonomy are protected; his dissent should be honored for research-only procedures, and the investigator notified.

checks.q: Researchers recruit only clients from a free clinic for a high-risk trial because they are easy to enroll. Which principle is violated?
checks.a: Justice, which requires fair selection and fair distribution of research burdens and benefits.

checks.q: A nurse wants to understand how older adults feel about telehealth visits. Which design fits best, and why?
checks.a: Qualitative, because the goal is to explore experience and meaning, producing themes rather than statistical measures.

topics.title: The Four Steps of EBP & Individual vs Organizational Implementation
topics.summary: EBP follows four steps: ask a focused clinical question (PICOT), retrieve the evidence, appraise it for validity, reliability, and clinical significance, then apply, evaluate, and disseminate it, either at one bedside or across an organization.
objectives: Distinguish background from foreground questions and classify clinical questions as diagnosis, therapy, etiology, or prognosis.
Write and deconstruct a PICOT question, identifying each element in a clinical scenario.
Differentiate primary, secondary, and review-of-literature sources and locate key information in each section of a research article.
Appraise evidence for validity, reliability, and clinical significance, and rank study designs on the hierarchy of evidence.
Interpret the ONS PEP stoplight ratings when deciding whether to use an intervention.
Describe how to apply, evaluate, accept, reject, or modify, and disseminate an evidence-based change, and relate the steps to the nursing process.
Contrast individual-nurse EBP with organizational EBP, and contrast an EBP project with a research study and with quality improvement.
topics.bigPicture:
The first two topics told you why evidence matters and how evidence is made. This topic is the workflow: what you actually do when you have a clinical question at 0300 or when your unit wants to fix a problem. The four steps are simple to list (ask, retrieve, appraise, apply) but each has a skill inside it that new nurses frequently get wrong: asking a question too broad to search, trusting a secondary summary as if it were the study, confusing “statistically significant” with “worth changing practice,” or trying to change a hospital policy alone.

The steps also map onto the nursing process you already know. Asking a question is assessment and diagnosis of a knowledge gap; retrieving and appraising evidence is planning; applying the change is implementation; and measuring outcomes is evaluation. If you can run the nursing process, you can run EBP.

On the NCLEX and in practice, the high-yield skills are: identify the parts of a PICOT question, rank evidence correctly (meta-analyses and RCTs at the top, individual and expert opinion at the bottom), interpret a stoplight rating, recognize that an evidence-based change must be evaluated after implementation, and know which changes a nurse can make independently and which require the organization’s policy process.

keyTerms.def: A knowledge-based, general question about a topic such as a disease or medication (“What is…?” “What does…?”), answered with textbooks, medical dictionaries, and drug handbooks.
A practice-based, narrow question about a specific clinical issue or intervention that affects client outcomes, answered with research studies.
A format for structuring a foreground question: Population/Problem, Intervention (or prognostic factor/exposure), Comparison, Outcome, and Time frame (optional). Also called PICO.
The common characteristics of the client group (age, gender, health problem) or the problem of interest.
What will be done to the population: a treatment, medication, therapy, new care routine, prognostic factor, or exposure.
The alternative against which the intervention is compared: standard care, placebo, no intervention, or a different intervention.
The measurable effect desired, such as symptom relief, fewer errors, shorter stay, or higher satisfaction.
The optional period needed to achieve or measure the outcome (for example, 12 hours, 4 weeks, 6 months).
A clinical question about selecting or interpreting diagnostic tests and their accuracy, safety, and cost-effectiveness.
A clinical question about selecting treatments that do more good than harm and lead to the best outcomes.
A clinical question about the causes of a condition or disease.
A clinical question about predicting the clinical course over time and possible complications.
The original published research article written by the investigators who conducted the study.
An article by one author that summarizes or discusses the original work of another author.
An article that presents the studies on a topic and ends with an evaluative statement or recommendation.
The concise summary of an entire research article, placed after the title.
The part of an article that describes in detail the study design, sample, tools, and procedures.
The part of an article that reports the statistical data, often with charts or tables.
The part of an article that summarizes and interprets the results in relation to the hypothesis and evaluates the findings.

Searchable collections of literature used to retrieve evidence, such as CINAHL, PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Database, EBSCO (DynaMed, PsycINFO), ScienceDirect, AHRQ, Evidence-Based Nursing (BMJ), and the Fuld Institute for EBP.
The degree to which a study measured what it intended to measure.
The ability of a study or tool to produce consistent results each time it is used.
Whether the difference found is large, useful, and meaningful enough to justify changing nursing practice.
A mathematical judgment (often p < 0.05) that a result is unlikely to be due to chance; it does not by itself show that the difference matters clinically.

Ranking of evidence by strength, from opinions based on experience (lowest) through expert opinion, non-experimental, quasi-experimental, and experimental studies, to meta-analyses and large RCTs (highest).
A method in which the results of a group of studies on a topic are combined and analyzed statistically as if they were one large study.

An experimental study in which participants are randomly assigned to an experimental group that receives the intervention or a control group that does not; the strongest single study design for showing cause and effect.
A study that tests an intervention but lacks random assignment or a true control group (for example, time-series or matched-control designs).
A study that observes without manipulating an intervention, including descriptive, correlational, and qualitative designs.
A study that compares people with a condition to people without it to identify factors that predict the condition; usually looks backward.
A longitudinal study that follows an exposed group and a non-exposed group over time to compare outcomes.
An in-depth report on a single individual, issue, or event.

The Oncology Nursing Society Putting Evidence into Practice system: green (recommended; strong evidence of effectiveness), yellow (not enough evidence to determine effectiveness or harm), red (strong evidence that the intervention is ineffective or possibly harmful).
Sharing EBP findings informally on the unit or agency, or formally through conference presentations and journal publication, completing the “EBP loop.”
A project that translates existing best evidence into practice to solve a specific local problem.
A formal investigation that generates new, generalizable knowledge using strict controls and IRB oversight.
A small-scale trial of a practice change on one unit or for a limited time to evaluate feasibility and outcomes before wider rollout.

sections.heading: The four-step map and Step 1: background versus foreground questions
sections.body:
Every EBP effort, whether one nurse wondering about a single client or a hospital redesigning a policy, follows the same four steps. Step 1: develop a focused clinical question. Step 2: retrieve the evidence. Step 3: evaluate (appraise) the evidence. Step 4: apply the evidence, evaluate the outcomes, and disseminate the findings.

These steps are a loop, not a line. After a change is applied, outcome data may raise a new question, starting the cycle again. They also parallel the nursing process, which helps you remember them and helps you answer “which step is the nurse in?” questions.

Not every question needs a research search. Background questions ask about general knowledge: “What is diabetic ketoacidosis?” “Who is at risk for hypoglycemia?” “What are the adverse effects of furosemide?” They fill a gap in your own knowledge and are answered with textbooks, medical dictionaries, and drug handbooks. New nurses ask many background questions; that is normal and safe.

Foreground questions are practice-based and narrow. They ask whether a specific intervention leads to a better outcome for a specific group: “How does using an incentive spirometer, compared with not using one, affect length of stay for surgical clients?” “How does a cooling blanket compare with antipyretic medication in reducing high fever?” These are answered with research studies. Foreground questions are what drive EBP changes.

Foreground questions fall into four categories. Classifying the question helps you choose the right study design to look for.

rows: Therapy
Which treatment does more good than harm and gives the best outcome?
Does chlorhexidine mouth care reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia compared with standard care?
RCTs and meta-analyses of RCTs
Diagnosis
How accurate, safe, and cost-effective is a test?
Is a bedside swallow screen as accurate as a video study in detecting aspiration after stroke?
Studies comparing the test with a reference standard
Etiology
What causes a condition, or what increases risk?
Does long-term proton pump inhibitor use increase hip fracture risk in older adults?
Cohort and case-control studies
Prognosis
What is the likely course or complication over time?
What proportion of clients with a first DVT have a recurrence within 2 years?
Cohort studies

check.q: A nurse asks, “What is the normal therapeutic range for a heparin infusion aPTT?” Background or foreground?
check.a: Background. It asks for general knowledge, answered with a drug reference or facility protocol, not a research search.

steps: Step 1, Ask (parallels assessment and diagnosis): notice a problem or knowledge gap and write a focused PICOT question.
Step 2, Retrieve (parallels planning): search databases for primary studies and reviews.
Step 3, Evaluate (parallels planning): appraise validity, reliability, and clinical significance, and rank the strength of the evidence.
Step 4, Apply, evaluate, and disseminate (parallels implementation and evaluation): integrate evidence, expertise, and preference; monitor outcomes; accept, reject, or modify; share the findings.

sections.heading: Building and taking apart a PICOT question
sections.body:
PICOT turns a vague worry into a searchable question. P is the population or problem (who, with what characteristics). I is the intervention, exposure, or prognostic factor of interest. C is the comparison: standard care, placebo, no intervention, or a different intervention. O is a measurable outcome. T, the time frame, is optional but helpful.

The most common errors: writing an outcome that cannot be measured (“feel better”), leaving out the comparison so there is nothing to test against, or confusing the intervention with the outcome. Practice deconstructing: “In adults receiving IV opioids after abdominal surgery (P), does continuous pulse oximetry and capnography monitoring (I) compared with intermittent spot checks (C) reduce rapid-response calls for respiratory depression (O) during the first 24 hours (T)?”

rows: P – Population/Problem
Who are the clients and what is their problem?
Adults after abdominal surgery
I – Intervention
What am I considering doing?
Incentive spirometer 10 times an hour while awake
C – Comparison
Compared with what?
Deep breathing and coughing without a spirometer
O – Outcome
What measurable result do I want?
Fewer postoperative pneumonias, shorter length of stay
T – Time frame
Over what period?
During the hospital stay (optional)

sections.example: Brent, a nurse educator, notices repeated procedural errors with IV pump programming among new medical-surgical nurses. His PICOT question: “In newly hired medical-surgical nurses (P), does simulation-based competency training (I) compared with standard lecture orientation (C) reduce pump-programming errors (O) over 6 months (T)?” Each element is specific enough to search and to measure.

check.q: Identify the C in this question: “For older adults with dementia in long-term care, does music therapy compared with usual activities reduce agitation episodes over 4 weeks?”
check.a: Usual activities. Music therapy is the intervention, reduced agitation episodes is the outcome, and 4 weeks is the time frame.

sections.heading: Step 2: Retrieve the evidence: sources, databases, and article anatomy
sections.body:
With a PICOT question, you search for evidence. A primary source is the original article written by the people who did the study; it is the most direct evidence. A secondary source is written by someone else summarizing or discussing that work (a news story, a magazine article, a colleague’s summary); it is useful for orientation but can misstate details. A review-of-literature article presents multiple studies on a topic and ends with an evaluative statement or recommendation. When accuracy matters, go to the primary source.

Databases make the search efficient. CINAHL (through EBSCO) is the core nursing and allied health database. PubMed/MEDLINE covers biomedical literature. The Cochrane Database holds systematic reviews. EBSCO also provides DynaMed (point-of-care summaries) and PsycINFO (behavioral science). ScienceDirect (Elsevier), AHRQ resources, Evidence-Based Nursing (BMJ), and the Fuld Institute for EBP round out the list. A general internet search or social media post is not a substitute.

Research articles follow a predictable order. Knowing it lets you find what you need quickly: read the abstract to decide whether the article is relevant, then the methods to judge how trustworthy it is, the results for the data, and the conclusion for the authors’ interpretation.

rows: 1. Title
The main topic of the study
Quick relevance screen
2. Abstract
Concise summary of the entire article
Decide whether to read the full article
3. Introduction
Question or focus, with background on earlier research
Understand why the study was done
4. Methods
Design, sample, tools, procedures in detail
Judge validity, reliability, and whether the sample resembles your clients
5. Results
Statistical data, charts, tables
See what was actually found
6. Conclusion
Interpretation of results relative to the hypothesis; evaluation of findings
See the authors’ meaning and limitations
7. References
Sources for more information
Find related primary studies

check.q: A nurse wants to know whether a study’s participants were similar to her clients in age and diagnosis. Which section should she read?
check.a: The methods section, which describes the sample, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and procedures.

sections.heading: Step 3: Appraise the evidence: validity, reliability, and clinical significance
sections.body:
Finding a study is not enough; you must decide whether to trust it and whether it matters. Three criteria anchor appraisal. Validity asks: did the study measure what it set out to measure? A study claiming to measure pain relief by counting how many times clients pressed the call light is weak on validity, because call-light use reflects many things besides pain. Reliability asks: would the method produce consistent results if repeated? A pain scale that gives very different scores when two nurses rate the same client is unreliable.

Clinical significance asks the practical question: is the difference big enough and useful enough to change what nurses do? A large study might find that a new dressing heals wounds a statistically significant half-day faster, but if it costs ten times as much and requires twice as many dressing changes, the difference may not be clinically significant. Statistical significance (a low p value) tells you the finding is unlikely to be chance; clinical significance tells you whether it matters to clients.

rows: Validity
Did it measure what it intended?
Outcome measured with an indirect or inappropriate tool; groups differ in important ways
Reliability
Are results consistent with repeated use?
Different observers get different results; tool not tested for consistency
Clinical significance
Is the difference meaningful enough to change practice?
Tiny effect, high cost, high burden, or outcome unimportant to clients

sections.analogy: Think of a bathroom scale. If it shows 150 pounds when you weigh 170, it is not valid (it is not measuring your true weight). If it shows 150, then 162, then 141 within a minute, it is not reliable (not consistent). Notice that a scale that reads exactly 150 every single time when you really weigh 170 is reliable but still not valid: consistency does not guarantee accuracy. A valid measure must be reliable, but a reliable measure is not automatically valid. Finally, if a diet makes the scale drop by 0.2 pounds in a month, that change may be real but is not clinically significant.

check.q: A study of 10,000 clients shows that a new oral-care product shortens average length of stay from 5.0 to 4.9 days (p = 0.04). It costs three times more than the current product and adds an extra oral-care session each shift. What should the nurse conclude?
check.a: The result is statistically significant (unlikely to be chance) but probably not clinically significant: a difference of about 2 hours in length of stay is too small to justify triple the cost and more nursing time, so it may not warrant changing practice.

sections.heading: Ranking evidence: the hierarchy, study designs, and the PEP stoplight
sections.body:
Not all evidence is equally strong. The hierarchy (Figure 45.3) ranks it from least to most powerful. At the bottom are opinions of individuals based on experience, then opinions of well-known experts and authorities. Above those are non-experimental studies (descriptive, correlational, qualitative), then quasi-experimental studies (time-series, matched control), then individual experimental studies, then meta-analyses of correlated studies. At the top, the gold standard, are large RCTs and meta-analyses of controlled studies.

Why are RCTs and meta-analyses at the top? Randomization spreads unknown differences evenly between groups, so a difference in outcome can be credited to the intervention (cause and effect). A meta-analysis pools many studies into one large analysis, increasing confidence. A cohort study follows exposed and unexposed groups forward over time; a case-control study starts with people who already have a condition and compares them with people who do not, looking back for predictors. Both are observational, useful for etiology and prognosis, but cannot prove cause the way an RCT can. A case study describes one person or event; it can generate ideas but not general conclusions.

Specialty organizations translate evidence into ratings. The Oncology Nursing Society’s Putting Evidence into Practice (PEP) uses a stoplight. Green: strong evidence supports the intervention as likely effective; use it. Yellow: not enough evidence to judge effectiveness or harm; use cautiously, with client preference and monitoring, or watch for new evidence. Red: strong evidence the intervention is ineffective or possibly harmful; avoid it and teach clients why.

rows: 1 (weakest)
Opinion based on individual experience
“In my experience, warm compresses help IV infiltration.”
Opinion of well-known experts or authorities
A respected specialist’s editorial or consensus statement
Non-experimental (descriptive, correlational, qualitative)
Survey of nurses’ hand-hygiene habits; interviews about living with heart failure
Quasi-experimental (time-series, matched control)
Fall rates before and after hourly rounding on one unit, no randomization
Individual experimental study
A single small randomized trial
Meta-analysis of correlated studies
Pooled analysis of several observational studies
7 (strongest)
Large RCTs and meta-analyses of controlled studies
Meta-analysis of 20 RCTs of chlorhexidine bathing in ICUs

check.q: A client with cancer asks about an herbal supplement that the PEP system rates red for fatigue. How should the nurse respond?
check.a: Explain that strong evidence shows it is likely ineffective or possibly harmful for fatigue, explore why the client is interested, and offer green-rated options (such as exercise) while notifying the provider of the client’s question. Respect the client’s autonomy while giving accurate information.

sections.heading: Step 4: Apply, evaluate, decide, and disseminate
sections.body:
Application is where evidence meets the client. The nurse combines the highest-rated evidence with clinical expertise and the client’s preferences. Then the change is monitored: is it being carried out the way the evidence describes (accurate replication), are the intended results happening, and are there unexpected outcomes? Based on the outcome data, the team decides to accept the change, reject it, or modify it.

The final piece, dissemination, closes the “EBP loop.” Findings may be shared informally (a unit huddle, a staff meeting, an agency newsletter) or formally (a poster or podium presentation at a national conference, an article in a professional journal). Dissemination prevents other units from repeating the same work and adds to nursing’s body of knowledge.
steps: Integrate the best evidence with assessment findings and client preferences into a specific plan.
Implement the change (for one client, or on a pilot unit for an organization).
Monitor fidelity: is the practice being done the way the evidence described?
Measure intended outcomes (for example, infection rate, length of stay, satisfaction) and watch for unexpected effects.
Decide: accept, reject, or modify based on the data.
Disseminate informally (unit, agency) or formally (conference, journal).

check.q: After a new oral-care protocol is adopted, pneumonia rates fall, but clients report more mouth soreness. What should the team do?
check.a: Evaluate the unexpected outcome and consider modifying the protocol (for example, a different product or technique) rather than simply accepting or abandoning it; outcome evaluation includes both intended and unintended effects.

sections.heading: Individual versus organizational EBP, and EBP versus research versus QI
sections.body:
EBP happens at two levels. An individual nurse uses EBP for clients in their own assignment: evaluating and adjusting personal nursing routines within existing scope and facility policy, and applying the result immediately at the bedside. Examples: using an evidence-based fall-risk tool more consistently, timing pain reassessment correctly, or using teach-back. The individual nurse cannot rewrite policy or adopt a practice that conflicts with policy, even if one study supports it.

Organizational EBP affects division-wide or hospital-wide protocols, policies, and procedures and therefore large client populations. It requires leadership approval, interprofessional committee work, stakeholder buy-in, and formal policy and procedure revision. It is rolled out through staff champions, continuing education, pilot testing, and ongoing quality and safety audits. The right team includes leadership (for authority and resources), staff development educators, frontline nurses (for clinical relevance and buy-in), a nurse manager, and a quality improvement specialist (for measurement).

Three related activities are often confused. A research study generates new, generalizable knowledge with strict controls and IRB oversight. An EBP project translates existing best evidence into practice to solve a local problem. Quality improvement (QI) uses local data and rapid cycles (such as Plan-Do-Study-Act) to improve a process in a specific setting. They work together: EBP supplies the best practice, QI measures and refines it locally, and research fills gaps where evidence is missing.

rows: Scope and focus
Specific clinical questions for clients in the nurse’s assignment
Division- or hospital-wide protocols affecting large populations
Decision and approval
Nurse evaluates and adjusts own routines within scope and existing policy
Leadership approval, interprofessional committee, stakeholder buy-in, formal policy revision
Execution and adoption
Immediate application at the bedside
Champions, continuing education, pilot testing, quality and safety audits
Example
Using teach-back for every discharge teaching session
Changing the hospital’s central-line dressing policy to chlorhexidine-impregnated dressings

sections.example: A night nurse reads a strong meta-analysis showing that a different IV-flush technique reduces catheter occlusions. Individually, she can refine her own technique only if it remains within current policy. To change the unit’s flush protocol, she brings the evidence to her nurse manager and the practice council, which reviews it, involves pharmacy and infection prevention, pilots it on one unit, audits occlusion rates, and then revises the policy.

check.q: Which of these is an EBP project rather than research: (a) randomizing 400 clients to two flush techniques to publish results, or (b) applying an existing guideline to reduce occlusions on one unit?
check.a: (b) is an EBP project: it applies existing evidence to a local problem. (a) is research because it generates new generalizable knowledge with controlled methods and would need IRB approval.

sections.heading: Common traps & look-alikes
sections.body: These distinctions appear repeatedly in EBP items. Match the clue in the stem to the concept.

General knowledge vs specific intervention-outcome question
“What is / what does” vs “compared with… does it improve…”
Intervention vs comparison
What is being tested vs what it is tested against
“New,” “using X” vs “standard care,” “placebo,” “usual”
Outcome vs intervention
The measurable result vs the action
“Reduce,” “decrease,” “rate of” usually marks the outcome
Primary vs secondary source
Original study by investigators vs someone else’s summary
“Written by the researchers who conducted…” vs “article describing a study”
Validity vs reliability
Measures the right thing vs gives consistent results
“Accurately measured” vs “same result each time”
Statistical vs clinical significance
Unlikely due to chance vs meaningful enough to change practice
“p < 0.05” vs “worth changing care, cost, size of benefit”
Cohort vs case-control
Follows exposed vs unexposed forward vs compares with/without condition looking back
“Followed for 10 years” vs “clients who developed X compared with those who did not”
Yellow vs red stoplight

Own practice within policy vs policy change requiring approval

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: steps, PICOT, and strength of evidence
sections.body:
Typical items ask you to (1) identify a PICOT element, (2) rank sources or designs by strength, (3) decide what to do with a rating or with mixed outcome data, (4) recognize the next step in the EBP process, or (5) choose the correct channel for a practice change. Distractors are usually one step out of order (implementing before appraising), one level off in the hierarchy (choosing a single quasi-experimental study over a meta-analysis of RCTs), or a confusion between individual and organizational action.

Sample item: A nurse on a surgical unit read a newspaper article reporting that a hospital in another state reduced surgical-site infections with a new preoperative skin-preparation routine. The nurse wants the unit to adopt it. Which action should the nurse take next? A. Begin using the routine for her own clients tomorrow. B. Locate and appraise the original study and related research before proposing a change. C. Ask the surgeons which routine they prefer. D. Write a new unit policy and post it in the break room.
steps: Read the stem: the nurse has a secondary source (a newspaper article) and wants a unit-wide change.
Identify what is being asked: the next step in the EBP process.
Spot cues: “newspaper article” = secondary source; “the unit to adopt it” = organizational change; nothing has been appraised yet.
Eliminate A: applying an unappraised practice that is not in policy skips Steps 2 and 3 and bypasses policy.
Eliminate C: what the surgeons prefer is opinion, which ranks near the bottom of the evidence hierarchy, and it does not answer whether the routine works.
Eliminate D: an individual nurse cannot write unit policy; organizational change requires approval, committees, and a pilot.
Choose B: retrieve the primary source and appraise the evidence (Steps 2 and 3) before any proposal goes to the practice council.

check.q: What reusable strategy fits “next step” EBP items?
check.a: Place the scenario on the four-step map (ask, retrieve, appraise, apply/evaluate/disseminate) and pick the option that is the very next step. Reject options that skip ahead (implement before appraising) or skip the organizational process.

sections.heading: Worked case: reducing catheter-associated urinary tract infections on 6 West
sections.body: You are a staff nurse on a 32-bed medical-surgical unit. The quality dashboard shows catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) rates twice the hospital benchmark. Your nurse manager asks you to join a small team. You notice that indwelling catheters often stay in for days after they are needed because removal requires a provider order. You recall hearing that some hospitals use nurse-driven catheter removal protocols.
steps: Step 1, ask: write the PICOT question. “In adult medical-surgical clients with indwelling urinary catheters (P), does a nurse-driven removal protocol (I) compared with provider-order-only removal (C) reduce CAUTI rates (O) over 6 months (T)?” This is a therapy question.

Step 2, retrieve: search CINAHL, PubMed, and the Cochrane Database for primary studies and systematic reviews; check AHRQ toolkits and professional guidelines. Read primary sources rather than relying on a vendor summary.

Step 3, appraise: you find a meta-analysis of controlled studies and several quasi-experimental before-and-after studies, all showing fewer catheter days and lower CAUTI rates. The meta-analysis is the strongest evidence. Check validity (were CAUTIs defined by standard surveillance criteria?), reliability (consistent results across hospitals?), and clinical significance (a meaningful drop in infections and catheter days).

Organizational process: because this changes a unit-wide protocol and the scope of nursing decisions, present the evidence to the nurse manager and practice council. Assemble an interprofessional team: a nursing leader, a staff development educator, frontline nurses, the nurse manager, a quality improvement specialist, infection prevention, and the provider group that must approve the protocol.

Step 4, apply: pilot the approved protocol on 6 West. Champions coach peers; educators teach the criteria for removal and bladder-scanning steps. Clients are told why their catheter may come out sooner and what to report.

Evaluate: audit adherence (fidelity), CAUTI rates, catheter days, and unexpected outcomes such as urinary retention requiring reinsertion. After 6 months CAUTIs fall 45%, but reinsertions rise slightly in post-op orthopedic clients; the team modifies the bladder-scan threshold for that group.
Disseminate: share results at a hospital nursing grand rounds, then spread the protocol to other units, and submit a poster to a national conference.

check.q: Why did the team not simply have each nurse start removing catheters without orders after reading the evidence?
check.a: Removing a catheter without an order or approved protocol is outside policy and could exceed the nurse’s authorized practice. Organizational EBP requires leadership approval, interprofessional agreement, and formal policy before nurses act on the new protocol.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
Under the NC Nursing Practice Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 90, Article 9A) and the RN components of practice in 21 NCAC 36 .0224, the RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment. That accountability shapes EBP in two ways. First, when a new evidence-based protocol is implemented, the RN still performs the assessment and evaluation for each client; the protocol supports nursing judgment but does not replace it. Second, the RN may delegate tasks that are part of a protocol (for example, a Nurse Aide I measuring and recording urine output, or a Nurse Aide II performing a listed advanced task) but may not delegate the nursing process or judgment, such as deciding that a catheter meets removal criteria.

In NC, a task must be on the aide’s approved list (Nurse Aide I registry kept by NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation; Nurse Aide II registry kept by NCBON) and the RN must decide delegation is appropriate for the specific client. The NCBON publishes a Decision Tree for Delegation to UAP and a scope-of-practice decision tree that RNs can use when a new protocol raises a question about who may perform a task.

When an organization adopts a nurse-driven protocol, the facility policy defines the authority, and the nurse must still practice within the scope defined by the Nurse Practice Act and NCBON rules.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 45 study guide, Evidence-Based Practice, learning outcomes 45.4 and 45.5, key terms and Sections 5–6, pp. 2763–2768 (including Tables 45.1–45.4, Figure 45.3, the ONS PEP stoplight system, the individual versus organizational comparison, and the Brent Calloway case synthesis).

Clarification 1 (hierarchy): The source’s hierarchy places “meta-analysis of correlated studies” below “large RCTs and meta-analyses of controlled studies.” Most current hierarchies (for example, Melnyk and Fineout-Overholt) place systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs at the very top and single RCTs just below; the guide teaches that a meta-analysis of RCTs is the strongest evidence and an RCT is the strongest single study design, consistent with the source.

Clarification 2 (statistical significance): The source defines clinical significance; this guide adds the contrast with statistical significance because confusion between them is a common appraisal error.

Clarification 3 (QI): The source contrasts an EBP project with a research study; this guide adds quality improvement (including Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles) as a third, related activity because NCLEX items often require distinguishing them.

Clarification 4 (PEP yellow): The source’s yellow-light wording (“not enough evidence to determine effectiveness, as harmful or helpful”) is taught as: insufficient evidence to determine whether the intervention is effective or harmful.

Clarification 5 (PEP categories): The three-color stoplight is a simplified teaching version. ONS Putting Evidence into Practice resources rate interventions in more detailed categories (from “recommended for practice” and “likely to be effective” through “effectiveness not established” to “effectiveness unlikely” and “not recommended for practice”), which group into the green, yellow, and red levels taught here. On an exam, translate the color or category into its meaning: strong evidence of benefit, not enough evidence, or strong evidence of no benefit or harm.

mnemonics.name: A-R-E-A: the four steps
mnemonics.text: Ask (PICOT) → Retrieve → Evaluate → Apply (then evaluate outcomes and disseminate). “Work in your AREA.”

mnemonics.name: Pyramid: “Only Experts Need Quiet Evenings, Mostly Reading”
mnemonics.text: Opinion → Expert → Non-experimental → Quasi-experimental → Experimental → Meta-analysis (correlated) → Randomized trials, large, and meta-analyses of controlled studies at the top.

mnemonics.name: Stoplight
mnemonics.text: Green = go (strong evidence it helps). Yellow = caution (not enough evidence). Red = stop (strong evidence it doesn’t help or harms).

pearls: A foreground question needs research; a background question needs a reference book or drug guide.
In PICOT, the C is what the intervention is compared with, often standard or usual care; the O must be measurable.
Read primary sources when the decision matters; a news story or summary is a secondary source.
Meta-analyses of RCTs and large RCTs are the strongest evidence; individual or expert opinion is the weakest.
Statistically significant does not automatically mean clinically significant.
After applying a change, evaluate outcomes and unexpected effects, then accept, reject, or modify.
An individual nurse may refine personal practice within policy; changing a protocol requires the organizational process.
An EBP project applies existing evidence locally; a research study creates new generalizable knowledge and needs an IRB.
redFlags: Implementing a practice change based on a single unappraised article, especially one that conflicts with current policy.
Using a red-rated (likely ineffective or harmful) intervention without discussing it with the client and provider.
Skipping outcome evaluation after a change: harmful unexpected effects may go undetected.
Delegating protocol decisions that require assessment or judgment (such as determining removal criteria) to unlicensed assistive personnel.
recap: Four steps: ask a clinical question, retrieve evidence, evaluate evidence, apply and evaluate outcomes, and disseminate.
Background questions use references; foreground questions use research and are written in PICOT format.
Clinical questions are classified as therapy, diagnosis, etiology, or prognosis.
Primary sources are the original studies; articles follow title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, conclusion, references.
Appraise for validity, reliability, and clinical significance; rank evidence from opinion (lowest) to meta-analysis and large RCTs (highest).
PEP stoplight: green use, yellow insufficient evidence, red avoid.
Individual EBP is immediate and within policy; organizational EBP requires approval, committees, pilots, champions, and audits.
The EBP steps parallel the nursing process.

checks.q: A nurse wonders whether chewing gum after bowel surgery shortens time to first flatus compared with standard care. Write the PICOT elements.
checks.a: P: adults after bowel surgery; I: chewing gum; C: standard care without gum; O: time to first flatus (return of bowel function); T: for example, the first 72 hours postoperatively.

checks.q: Two sources disagree: an expert panel opinion and a meta-analysis of 12 RCTs. Which should guide the unit protocol, and why?
checks.a: The meta-analysis of RCTs, the highest level of evidence. Expert opinion ranks near the bottom of the hierarchy.

checks.q: A pilot of a new early-mobility protocol shows no change in length of stay but a rise in falls. What is the appropriate decision?
checks.a: Reject or modify the change; outcome data show no benefit and an unexpected harm. The team would investigate and either revise the protocol or discontinue it.

checks.q: A nurse uses teach-back with every client she discharges after reading strong evidence. Does she need committee approval?
checks.a: No. Using an evidence-based communication technique within existing policy and scope is individual-nurse EBP. A change to a unit-wide protocol would need the organizational process.

checks.q: A study reports a pain tool gives the same score when two nurses rate the same client. What quality does this show?
checks.a: Reliability (consistency). It does not by itself show validity, which is whether the tool actually measures pain.

checks.q: A team wants to test a brand-new device on clients and publish whether it works better than current care. Is this an EBP project?
checks.a: No, it is research. It generates new generalizable knowledge and requires IRB review and informed consent from participants.
